title: Oxygen-delivery devices
body: Oxygen-delivery devices Respiratory Support Clinical overview Choose the least invasive device that reliably achieves the prescribed saturation target and work-of-breathing goal. Escalate based on physiology, not device sequence alone. Initial stabilization Position airway, suction as needed, apply continuous pulse oximetry and reassess after each device change. Low-flow nasal cannula is useful for mild oxygen need; simple/venturi masks provide higher or controlled FiO₂; non-rebreather is a short bridge for severe hypoxemia while definitive support is prepared. Disease-specific treatment / settings Humidify prolonged higher-flow oxygen. Use an oxygen blender when precise FiO₂ is required, especially in neonates or congenital heart disease. Monitoring SpO₂ trend, respiratory rate, retractions, mental status, heart rate and gas exchange when clinically indicated. Expected response Reduced work of breathing and stable saturation on a lower or unchanged FiO₂. Failure criteria and escalation Rising oxygen requirement, exhaustion, apnea, hypercapnia, altered consciousness or poor perfusion. Complications / cautions Pressure injury, mucosal drying, delayed escalation and excessive oxygen exposure in susceptible patients. Sources and local verification RCUK 2025 Paediatric Life Support; local respiratory therapy policy. title: High-flow nasal cannula
body: High-flow nasal cannula Respiratory Support Clinical overview Use for hypoxemic respiratory failure or increased work of breathing when low-flow oxygen is insufficient and the child can protect the airway. HFNC provides heated humidified flow, dead-space washout and variable distending pressure; it is not equivalent to controlled CPAP. Initial stabilization Ensure appropriate cannula size with nares not fully occluded. Common starting flow is approximately 1–2 L/kg/min in infants and young children, with local maximums; start FiO₂ to stabilize then titrate down. Obtain senior/PCCU review before or soon after initiation in a deteriorating child. Disease-specific treatment / settings Treat the cause concurrently: bronchodilator for bronchospasm, antibiotics when bacterial infection is suspected, secretion clearance where appropriate. Do not use HFNC to delay intubation in apnea, severe encephalopathy, shock or rapidly progressive failure. Monitoring Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring; reassess within 30–60 minutes for HR, RR, retractions, FiO₂ and mental status. Expected response Meaningful reduction in tachypnea, retractions and heart rate, with stable/improving oxygenation. Failure criteria and escalation No improvement within the planned reassessment window, FiO₂ requirement rising toward 0.60 or more, recurrent apnea, worsening hypercapnia/acidosis or hemodynamic instability. Complications / cautions Air leak, abdominal distension, pressure injury, secretion obstruction and false reassurance. Sources and local verification RCH HFNP guideline; institutional bronchiolitis/HFNC pathway; RCUK 2025 PLS. title: CPAP and BiPAP basics
body: CPAP and BiPAP basics Respiratory Support Clinical overview CPAP improves oxygenation and splints airways; BiPAP adds inspiratory pressure support to improve ventilation. Best suited to a cooperative child with intact airway reflexes and reversible respiratory failure. Initial stabilization Use experienced staff, correct interface and continuous monitoring. Typical editable starting points: CPAP 5–8 cmH₂O; BiPAP EPAP 5–8 and IPAP 8–12 cmH₂O, then titrate to response and local protocol. Disease-specific treatment / settings Treat agitation non-pharmacologically first; sedation can precipitate airway loss and requires PCCU-level monitoring. Provide gastric decompression if significant distension. Monitoring SpO₂, respiratory effort, synchrony, leak, skin pressure points, blood gas and hemodynamics. Expected response Improved ventilation/oxygenation, lower work of breathing and good patient-device synchrony. Failure criteria and escalation Inability to protect airway, copious secretions, recurrent vomiting, worsening acidosis, shock, apnea or intolerance despite optimization. Complications / cautions Aspiration, pressure injury, gastric distension, air leak and delayed intubation. Sources and local verification RCUK 2025 PLS; local NIV policy. title: Non-invasive ventilation troubleshooting
body: Non-invasive ventilation troubleshooting Respiratory Support Clinical overview Troubleshoot in a fixed sequence: patient, interface, circuit, settings, then disease progression. Initial stabilization Check airway patency, secretion burden, mask position, leak, exhalation port, humidification and circuit disconnection. Confirm trigger sensitivity, rise time, backup rate and inspiratory/expiratory pressures match the child. Disease-specific treatment / settings Correct agitation drivers such as hypoxemia, pain, fever, urinary retention and mask discomfort. Escalate rather than repeatedly increasing pressures when physiology worsens. Monitoring Waveforms, delivered tidal volume, leak percentage, SpO₂, RR, gas exchange and mental status. Expected response Improved synchrony and lower work of breathing after the identified issue is corrected. Failure criteria and escalation Persistent large leak, poor synchrony, worsening gas, declining consciousness, apnea or shock. Complications / cautions Barotrauma, gastric insufflation, pressure injury and delayed invasive ventilation. Sources and local verification Local ventilator/NIV manual; RCUK 2025 PLS. title: Indications for intubation
body: Indications for intubation Respiratory Support Clinical overview Intubate for failure of oxygenation, ventilation or airway protection, or when anticipated deterioration makes controlled airway management safer than rescue intubation. Initial stabilization Call experienced airway/PCCU/anesthesia support early and use a checklist. Preoxygenate with the best tolerated method, optimize hemodynamics and prepare backup airway plans. Disease-specific treatment / settings Common triggers: refractory hypoxemia, severe hypercapnic acidosis with fatigue, recurrent apnea, GCS decline, uncontrolled status epilepticus, shock requiring airway control, or upper-airway obstruction. Monitoring Continuous ECG, SpO₂, BP and waveform capnography; document first-pass success and complications. Expected response Confirmed tube position with sustained waveform capnography and improved oxygenation/ventilation. Failure criteria and escalation Failed first attempt, severe desaturation, hypotension, bradycardia, cannot intubate/cannot oxygenate. Complications / cautions Hypoxemia, hypotension, bradycardia, aspiration, esophageal or mainstem intubation and airway trauma. Sources and local verification RCUK 2025 PLS; Difficult Airway Society pediatric guidance; local RSI protocol. title: Pediatric rapid-sequence intubation
body: Pediatric rapid-sequence intubation Respiratory Support Clinical overview Pediatric RSI is a high-risk team procedure. Use a checklist, role assignment, physiologic optimization and explicit plans A–D. Initial approach / settings Preoxygenate with the most effective tolerated method; use apneic oxygenation when feasible. Prepare appropriately sized cuffed tubes, video/direct laryngoscope, bougie/stylet, suction, BVM with PEEP, rescue supraglottic airway and surgical airway equipment. Estimate cuffed ETT size age/4 + 3.5 mm for children over 1 year, but prepare one size above/below and use length/weight references in infants. Medication doses / settings Ketamine 1–2 mg/kg IV is commonly used for induction when hemodynamic stability is desired; lower dose may be appropriate in shock. Rocuronium 1–1.2 mg/kg IV provides rapid paralysis. Succinylcholine 1–2 mg/kg IV may be used when not contraindicated. Use atropine selectively rather than routinely; dose and indication should follow current PALS/local policy. Monitoring intervals Continuous ECG, SpO2, BP cycling rapidly and waveform capnography. Confirm tube with sustained ETCO2, chest rise, bilateral air entry and imaging as appropriate. Failure criteria and escalation Falling saturation, failed first attempt, cannot intubate/cannot oxygenate, hemodynamic collapse or absent capnography. Move promptly through the difficult-airway plan. Complications / cautions Peri-intubation hypoxemia, hypotension, bradycardia, aspiration, esophageal/mainstem intubation and barotrauma. Begin post-intubation analgesia/sedation immediately. Sources and local verification Current PALS/RCUK pediatric life support; institutional difficult-airway and RSI protocol. title: Initial ventilator settings by disease
body: Initial ventilator settings by disease Respiratory Support Clinical overview Start with disease-pattern settings, then individualize using ideal body weight, gas exchange, mechanics and hemodynamics. Initial stabilization Confirm ETT position, obtain chest movement and waveform capnography, then set lung-protective ventilation. Use the dedicated ventilator calculator for editable starting suggestions. Disease-specific treatment / settings Obstructive disease: lower RR and long expiratory time. Restrictive/ARDS: lower tidal volume and adequate PEEP. Neuromuscular disease: support minute ventilation and secretion clearance. Monitoring Peak/plateau pressures, expiratory flow returning to baseline, tidal volume, ETCO₂, gas, SpO₂ and BP. Expected response Acceptable oxygenation/ventilation without excessive pressure, auto-PEEP or hemodynamic compromise. Failure criteria and escalation Rising pressures, worsening acidosis, persistent hypoxemia, air trapping, hypotension or dyssynchrony. Complications / cautions Volutrauma, barotrauma, atelectrauma, oxygen toxicity and ventilator-induced hypotension. Sources and local verification PALICC-2 pediatric ARDS guidance; RCUK 2025 PLS; local ventilation protocol. title: Ventilator alarm troubleshooting
body: Ventilator alarm troubleshooting Respiratory Support Clinical overview Respond to the patient first, not the alarm; disconnect and hand-ventilate if the child is unstable and equipment failure is possible. Initial stabilization High pressure: consider DOPE—displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax, equipment—plus bronchospasm and biting. Low pressure/volume: circuit disconnect, cuff leak, extubation or large airway leak. Disease-specific treatment / settings Pass suction catheter to assess patency; examine chest symmetry and tube depth; use bedside ultrasound/chest radiograph as indicated. Monitoring SpO₂, ETCO₂ waveform, airway pressures, delivered/exhaled volumes and hemodynamics. Expected response Alarm resolves with stable gas exchange and identified cause corrected. Failure criteria and escalation Cannot ventilate, absent ETCO₂, unilateral breath sounds with instability, tension pneumothorax signs or persistent severe hypoxemia. Complications / cautions Delayed recognition of tube displacement, pneumothorax or circuit failure. Sources and local verification RCUK 2025 PLS; local ventilator troubleshooting policy. title: Weaning and extubation-readiness checklist
body: Weaning and extubation-readiness checklist Respiratory Support Clinical overview Extubation readiness requires improvement in disease, adequate gas exchange on modest support, airway protection and a feasible post-extubation plan. Initial stabilization Review sedation, secretions, cough strength, airway edema risk, hemodynamics and neuromuscular function. Perform a spontaneous breathing trial according to local protocol when appropriate. Disease-specific treatment / settings Consider dexamethasone before extubation when high risk for airway edema; ensure rescue equipment and NIV/HFNC plan are ready. Monitoring Work of breathing, tidal volume, RR, gas, secretion burden, leak assessment where used and neurologic status. Expected response Comfortable spontaneous breathing with stable gas exchange and hemodynamics. Failure criteria and escalation Marked tachypnea, apnea, rising CO₂, poor cough, excessive secretions or hemodynamic instability during trial. Complications / cautions Extubation failure, upper-airway obstruction, atelectasis and withdrawal/agitation. Sources and local verification Local extubation protocol; RCUK 2025 PLS. title: Post-extubation stridor
body: Post-extubation stridor Respiratory Support Clinical overview Suspect laryngeal edema when inspiratory stridor and increased work of breathing occur after extubation. Initial stabilization Position, humidified oxygen, minimize agitation and assess severity immediately. Prepare reintubation equipment early in severe or progressive obstruction. Disease-specific treatment / settings Nebulized epinephrine is commonly used for moderate/severe stridor; corticosteroid treatment depends on timing and local protocol. Heliox may be a temporary bridge where available. Monitoring Continuous SpO₂, air entry, stridor at rest, retractions, mental status and response after each treatment. Expected response Reduced stridor and work of breathing with stable oxygenation. Failure criteria and escalation Silent chest, fatigue, cyanosis, altered consciousness, poor air entry or recurrent severe symptoms after epinephrine. Complications / cautions Rapid airway loss and delayed reintubation. Sources and local verification Local post-extubation airway pathway; RCUK 2025 PLS. title: Difficult airway escalation
body: Difficult airway escalation Respiratory Support Clinical overview Declare difficulty early, limit repeated attempts and prioritize oxygenation over tracheal intubation. Initial stabilization Call anesthesia/ENT/PCCU and bring the difficult-airway cart. Use the most experienced operator, optimize position and move deliberately through Plan A/B/C/D. Disease-specific treatment / settings Consider video laryngoscopy, bougie/stylet and supraglottic airway. In cannot-intubate/cannot-oxygenate physiology, proceed to the institution’s emergency front-of-neck access pathway. Monitoring Time, attempts, saturation nadir, ventilation between attempts and hemodynamics. Expected response Oxygenation maintained and airway secured with the least traumatic method. Failure criteria and escalation Two failed attempts by experienced operators, inability to mask ventilate or falling saturation despite rescue maneuvers. Complications / cautions Airway trauma, edema, hypoxic arrest and task fixation. Sources and local verification Difficult Airway Society pediatric algorithm; local difficult-airway plan. title: Accidental extubation response
body: Accidental extubation response Respiratory Support Clinical overview Treat as an airway emergency; determine immediately whether the child can oxygenate and ventilate without the tube. Initial stabilization Call for help, stop feeds, position airway, suction and provide bag-mask ventilation with PEEP as needed. Do not blindly advance a partially displaced tube. Disease-specific treatment / settings Reintubate when respiratory failure persists or airway protection is inadequate; prepare full RSI and difficult-airway backup. Monitoring SpO₂, ETCO₂, HR, BP and chest movement; document event and contributing factors. Expected response Stable spontaneous breathing or successful reintubation with confirmed ETCO₂. Failure criteria and escalation Inability to ventilate, severe desaturation, bradycardia or hemodynamic collapse. Complications / cautions Hypoxic injury, aspiration and repeated displacement. Sources and local verification Local unplanned extubation policy; RCUK 2025 PLS. title: Severe asthma
body: Severe asthma Disease-Specific Respiratory Pathways Clinical overview Severe asthma is defined by persistent respiratory distress, poor air entry, hypoxemia, exhaustion or inadequate response to initial inhaled bronchodilator therapy. A quiet chest can represent critical obstruction. Consider alternative/complicating diagnoses: anaphylaxis, foreign body, pneumonia, pneumothorax, cardiac disease and vocal-cord dysfunction. Initial approach / settings Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring, frequent respiratory examination and early PCCU/RT involvement. Give oxygen to the prescribed saturation target; use inhaled salbutamol/albuterol promptly and add ipratropium during the initial severe phase. Give systemic corticosteroid early; do not delay for imaging. Medication doses / settings Continuous nebulized salbutamol/albuterol is institution-specific; common pediatric pathways use weight-banded continuous delivery with close potassium, glucose, lactate and rhythm monitoring. Ipratropium 250–500 micrograms nebulized every 20 minutes for three doses is commonly used in severe exacerbations, depending on age/weight and local protocol. Magnesium sulfate IV 25–50 mg/kg over about 20–30 minutes (commonly maximum 2 g) for severe disease not responding to initial therapy. Aminophylline, IV salbutamol/terbutaline and ketamine are rescue therapies requiring PCCU/pharmacy protocol and toxicity monitoring. Respiratory support HFNC may improve oxygenation but does not reliably relieve severe airflow obstruction; excessive flow can worsen dynamic hyperinflation in some patients. NIV may be considered in a cooperative child with preserved airway reflexes and close expert monitoring; do not delay intubation in exhaustion, altered consciousness, refractory hypoxemia or shock. Monitoring intervals Reassess continuously during initial stabilization and at least every 15–30 minutes after major therapy changes. Trend air entry, speech, accessory muscle use, mental status, heart rate, SpO2, blood gas when indicated, potassium, glucose and lactate. Failure criteria and escalation Worsening fatigue, bradycardia, altered mental status, rising PaCO2 with acidosis, recurrent apnea, hemodynamic compromise or refractory hypoxemia. Prepare for a physiologically difficult intubation with senior airway/PCCU/anesthesia support and a post-intubation ventilation plan. Complications / cautions Dynamic hyperinflation, auto-PEEP, barotrauma, hypotension, hypokalemia, lactic acidosis and tachyarrhythmia. After intubation use low respiratory rate, long expiratory time, cautious tidal volume and permissive hypercapnia when appropriate; accept incomplete normalization to avoid air trapping. Sources and local verification CPS acute asthma guidance; institutional severe asthma pathway; current PALS/PCCU protocol. title: Bronchiolitis requiring HFNC
body: Bronchiolitis requiring HFNC Disease-Specific Respiratory Pathways Clinical overview HFNC is considered when bronchiolitis causes persistent hypoxemia or moderate/severe work of breathing despite suction, positioning and low-flow oxygen. Routine bronchodilators, corticosteroids and antibiotics are not indicated unless another diagnosis or a documented trial supports them. Initial approach / settings Gentle nasal suction, minimal handling, hydration assessment and enteral/NG feeding when safe. Select cannula that does not fully occlude the nares. Common initial flow is 1–2 L/kg/min with institutional maximums; titrate FiO2 to the local saturation target. Monitoring intervals Continuous SpO2/heart rate and documented reassessment within 30–60 minutes of initiation or escalation. Track respiratory rate, retractions, apnea, mental status, FiO2, feeding tolerance and hydration. Expected response Lower heart and respiratory rates, reduced retractions and stable oxygenation without rising FiO2. Failure criteria and escalation No meaningful improvement within 30–60 minutes, recurrent apnea, exhaustion, rising CO2/acidosis, FiO2 around 0.60 or greater, or hemodynamic instability. Escalate to CPAP/NIV or intubation based on physiology and local PCCU capability. Complications / cautions Air leak, abdominal distension, skin injury, delayed escalation and fluid overload. Sources and local verification CPS bronchiolitis guidance; RCH HFNC guidance; local respiratory therapy pathway. title: Severe pneumonia
body: Severe pneumonia Disease-Specific Respiratory Pathways Clinical overview Consider bacterial, viral, aspiration and complicated pneumonia; assess for effusion, empyema, necrosis and sepsis. Initial stabilization Oxygen/respiratory support, cultures when feasible before antibiotics, prompt empiric antimicrobials and fluid/perfusion assessment. Use ultrasound or chest imaging when complications are suspected. Disease-specific treatment / settings Antibiotic choice should follow age, immunization, local resistance, MRSA risk and aspiration context. Drain significant complicated effusion/empyema with respiratory/surgical/interventional input. Monitoring SpO₂, work of breathing, perfusion, lactate, urine output, inflammatory markers and imaging trajectory when complicated. Expected response Falling oxygen need, improved work of breathing and perfusion within the expected interval. Failure criteria and escalation Escalating support, shock, rising lactate, enlarging effusion, air leak or multiorgan dysfunction. Complications / cautions Empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, pneumothorax, ARDS and septic shock. Sources and local verification IDSA/PIDS pediatric CAP guidance; local antimicrobial and empyema pathways. title: Pediatric ARDS
body: Pediatric ARDS Disease-Specific Respiratory Pathways Clinical overview Use PALICC-2 concepts: acute pulmonary disease with hypoxemia and new infiltrates not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload. Severity and trajectory should be assessed using oxygenation index/oxygen saturation index when invasively ventilated. Initial approach / settings Treat the cause, use lung-protective ventilation and avoid unnecessary positive fluid balance after shock is corrected. Use ideal/predicted body weight for tidal-volume targets. Start approximately 6–8 mL/kg for preserved compliance and 4–6 mL/kg when compliance is poor, then titrate to pressures and gas exchange. Use PEEP/FiO2 strategy appropriate to severity; limit plateau and driving pressure according to local PALICC-based protocol. Monitoring intervals Continuous oxygenation/hemodynamics; serial gases, ventilator waveforms, plateau pressure, compliance, fluid balance and OI/OSI. Reassess after every major PEEP, tidal-volume or recruitment change. Failure criteria and escalation Progressive OI/OSI, severe hypoxemia despite optimized PEEP, injurious pressures, worsening shock or inability to ventilate. Consider prone positioning, neuromuscular blockade for severe dyssynchrony, inhaled pulmonary vasodilator as rescue, and early ECMO-center discussion when refractory. Complications / cautions Ventilator-induced lung injury, air leak, hemodynamic compromise, sedation/NMBA complications, delirium and critical illness weakness. Sources and local verification PALICC-2 pediatric ARDS guidance; local ventilation and ECMO referral pathways. title: Croup requiring advanced airway support
body: Croup requiring advanced airway support Disease-Specific Respiratory Pathways Clinical overview Severe croup includes stridor at rest with marked retractions, fatigue, hypoxemia or reduced air entry. Initial stabilization Keep the child calm, provide dexamethasone and nebulized epinephrine, and involve anesthesia/ENT/PCCU early. Avoid upsetting examinations or procedures until the airway team is ready. Disease-specific treatment / settings Prepare a smaller-than-age-predicted ETT because of subglottic edema; use the most experienced airway operator. Monitoring Continuous SpO₂, stridor, air entry, mental status and recurrence after epinephrine. Expected response Sustained reduction in stridor and work of breathing after observation. Failure criteria and escalation Exhaustion, cyanosis, altered consciousness, poor air entry or recurrent severe obstruction. Complications / cautions Rapid airway obstruction, post-intubation edema and unplanned extubation. Sources and local verification RCH croup guideline; local difficult-airway protocol. title: Upper-airway obstruction
body: Upper-airway obstruction Disease-Specific Respiratory Pathways Clinical overview Differentiate croup, anaphylaxis, epiglottitis/bacterial tracheitis, foreign body, abscess and post-extubation edema. Initial stabilization Call anesthesia/ENT/PCCU early, keep the child upright and calm, and avoid airway agitation. Give condition-specific therapy such as IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis or nebulized epinephrine/dexamethasone for croup. Disease-specific treatment / settings Do not force throat examination when epiglottitis or critical obstruction is suspected. Prepare for controlled airway management in the operating room/PICU when feasible. Monitoring Stridor, voice, drooling, air entry, mental status, SpO₂ and hemodynamics. Expected response Improving air entry and reduced stridor without fatigue. Failure criteria and escalation Silent obstruction, cyanosis, bradycardia, altered consciousness or inability to maintain oxygenation. Complications / cautions Complete obstruction, aspiration and traumatic airway attempts. Sources and local verification RCUK 2025 PLS; local ENT/difficult-airway pathway. title: Aspiration
body: Aspiration Disease-Specific Respiratory Pathways Clinical overview Aspiration may cause acute obstruction, chemical pneumonitis, bacterial pneumonia or ARDS. Initial stabilization Suction visible material, support oxygenation/ventilation and evaluate for foreign body or ongoing aspiration. Bronchoscopy is indicated when particulate obstruction or foreign body is suspected. Disease-specific treatment / settings Antibiotics are not automatically required for uncomplicated chemical pneumonitis; use when bacterial infection is suspected or established. Monitoring SpO₂, work of breathing, fever, gas exchange and radiographic progression when severe. Expected response Improving oxygenation and respiratory effort over hours with supportive care. Failure criteria and escalation Persistent focal obstruction, worsening oxygen requirement, shock or evolving ARDS. Complications / cautions Pneumonia, abscess, ARDS and recurrent aspiration. title: Pulmonary hemorrhage
body: Pulmonary hemorrhage Disease-Specific Respiratory Pathways Clinical overview Treat frank airway bleeding with hypoxemia as a life-threatening airway and circulation emergency. Initial stabilization Call PCCU/respiratory/hematology, give high-concentration oxygen, secure airway if needed and correct coagulopathy. Use large-bore suction and isolate the bleeding lung when anatomically possible. Disease-specific treatment / settings Ventilation may require higher PEEP; bronchoscopy/interventional radiology/surgery may be required. Review anticoagulants, platelet count, coagulation, vasculitis and cardiac causes. Monitoring Hemoglobin, coagulation, gas exchange, airway pressures, hemodynamics and bleeding volume. Expected response Bleeding slows, oxygenation stabilizes and transfusion requirement falls. title: Recognition of pediatric shock
body: Recognition of pediatric shock Shock & Vasoactives Clinical overview Recognition of pediatric shock requires classification of preload, contractility, afterload and obstruction before repeated treatment. title: Septic shock
body: Septic shock Shock & Vasoactives Clinical overview Septic shock is infection-associated cardiovascular dysfunction with abnormal perfusion, hypotension or need for vasoactive support. Hypotension is a late sign in children. Initial approach / settings Obtain cultures when feasible without delaying antimicrobials. Give broad-spectrum antibiotics as rapidly as possible for shock. Use balanced crystalloid in cautious 10–20 mL/kg aliquots with reassessment after each aliquot where ICU support is available; stop for hepatomegaly, crackles, worsening oxygenation or other overload signs. Start vasoactive support early when shock persists after limited fluid or when fluid intolerance is present; peripheral initiation is acceptable with close site monitoring while central access is arranged. Medication doses / settings Epinephrine is commonly favored for cold/low-output physiology; norepinephrine for vasodilated/warm shock. Start and titrate using local concentration and dose protocol. Correct hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia and adrenal insufficiency when clinically indicated; consider hydrocortisone for catecholamine-resistant shock with suspected adrenal dysfunction. Monitoring intervals Reassess perfusion every 5–15 minutes during resuscitation: mental status, pulses, capillary refill, extremity temperature, BP, urine output and lactate trend. Use bedside ultrasound/echo and dynamic response rather than static signs alone when available. Failure criteria and escalation Persistent abnormal perfusion, rising lactate, oliguria, myocardial dysfunction, escalating vasoactives or multi-organ dysfunction. Escalate to invasive monitoring, advanced vasoactive strategy, ventilation and ECMO discussion as appropriate. Sources and local verification Surviving Sepsis Campaign pediatric guidance; local antimicrobial and vasoactive protocols. title: Vasoactive selection
body: Vasoactive selection Shock & Vasoactives Clinical overview Choose vasoactive support from the dominant physiology and reassess frequently; phenotype may evolve during resuscitation. Correct hypoxemia, acidosis, hypoglycemia, ionized hypocalcemia and inadequate preload while avoiding fluid overload. Agent selection Epinephrine: low cardiac output/cold shock or myocardial dysfunction; watch tachyarrhythmia, hyperglycemia and lactate. Norepinephrine: vasodilatory/warm shock with low systemic vascular resistance; watch ischemia and excessive afterload. Dobutamine or milrinone: selected low-output states with adequate blood pressure; both may worsen hypotension. Vasopressin: rescue adjunct for refractory vasoplegia under PCCU guidance, not routine first-line therapy. Administration Start through a well-functioning peripheral or intraosseous line when delay to central access would be harmful; use a dedicated line, frequent site checks and institutional concentration. Titrate every few minutes to perfusion and blood-pressure goals using smart-pump guardrails and independent double-check. Monitoring intervals Continuous ECG and BP; reassess capillary refill, pulses, mental status, urine output and lactate/perfusion trend every 5–15 minutes during active titration. Failure criteria and escalation Escalating dose, persistent oliguria/lactate, arrhythmia, ischemia or multi-organ dysfunction requires echo-guided reassessment and advanced PCCU support. Sources and local verification Surviving Sepsis Campaign pediatric guidance; institutional vasoactive concentration and peripheral-infusion policy. title: Status epilepticus
body: Status epilepticus Neurologic Emergencies Clinical overview Convulsive status epilepticus is a seizure lasting 5 minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery. Treat while evaluating glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium, infection, trauma, toxins and adherence. Medication doses / settings First-line: lorazepam IV 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg), midazolam IN/IM/buccal 0.2 mg/kg (local maximum), or diazepam according to route-specific protocol. Count prehospital benzodiazepines to avoid excessive stacking. If ongoing after adequate benzodiazepine therapy, give one second-line agent promptly: levetiracetam 40–60 mg/kg IV (common max 4.5 g), fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (max 1.5 g PE), or valproate 20–40 mg/kg when not contraindicated. Refractory status requires PCCU/neurology, airway preparation, continuous EEG and anesthetic infusion protocol such as midazolam; ketamine or pentobarbital may be used in specialist pathways. Monitoring intervals Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring, bedside glucose immediately, serial neurologic examination and temperature. Obtain EEG urgently if paralysis is used or nonconvulsive status is suspected. Failure criteria and escalation Seizure persists after benzodiazepine plus appropriate second-line medication, recurrent seizures without recovery, respiratory failure, shock or concern for raised ICP. Complications / cautions Respiratory depression, hypotension, aspiration, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and medication-specific dysrhythmia/hepatotoxicity. Sources and local verification CPS convulsive status epilepticus guidance; current PALS and institutional neurology/PCCU pathway. title: Raised intracranial pressure
body: Raised intracranial pressure Neurologic Emergencies Clinical overview Suspect raised ICP with declining consciousness, focal deficits, abnormal pupils, repeated vomiting, hypertension/bradycardia, irregular respirations or posturing. Normal vital signs do not exclude it. Initial approach / settings Call PCCU/neurosurgery, elevate head 30 degrees, keep neck midline, avoid fever, hypoxemia, hypotension and hypo-osmolar fluids. Secure the airway when necessary using a hemodynamically protective plan; target normoxia and generally normocapnia. Brief controlled hyperventilation is only a temporizing measure for impending herniation. Medication doses / settings Hypertonic saline 3% 2–5 mL/kg IV over 10–20 minutes is commonly used for acute intracranial hypertension; repeat/infusion strategy requires specialist protocol. Mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg IV may be considered when hemodynamics and renal status permit. Treat seizures promptly and maintain adequate analgesia/sedation. Monitoring intervals Frequent GCS/pupils, BP, sodium/osmolality, urine output and ventilation. Reassess immediately after osmotherapy. Failure criteria and escalation Progressive pupillary change, posturing, refractory ICP, worsening CT findings or hemodynamic instability. Complications / cautions Hypotension, hypernatremia, osmotic diuresis, renal injury and rebound ICP. Avoid routine corticosteroids in traumatic brain injury. Sources and local verification CPS acute head trauma guidance; Brain Trauma Foundation pediatric severe TBI guidance; local neurocritical care protocol. title: Sedation by procedure
body: Sedation by procedure Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis How to use this section Choose the procedure first, then define whether the child needs analgesia, anxiolysis/sedation, immobility, or all three. Paralysis never substitutes for analgesia or sedation. Before moderate/deep sedation: confirm weight, allergies, airway risk, fasting status when applicable, IV access/rescue plan, monitoring, suction, oxygen/BVM and a clinician capable of airway rescue. Lumbar puncture Analgesia: topical anesthetic when time allows plus local lidocaine infiltration. Add comfort positioning, distraction and child-life support when available. Sedation: a cooperative older child may need none or minimal anxiolysis; for deeper sedation, ketamine is useful because it supplies both dissociation and analgesia. Propofol provides sedation but no analgesia and requires a separate analgesic/local-anesthetic plan. Paralysis: not indicated for routine lumbar puncture. Intubation / RSI Analgesia/sympathetic blunting: fentanyl may be used selectively and slowly when physiology permits; do not delay an urgent airway to give it. Induction: ketamine is commonly favored when hypotension/bronchospasm is a concern; propofol is rapid but can markedly lower blood pressure; etomidate is hemodynamically stable but has adrenal-suppression considerations. Paralysis: rocuronium 1–1.2 mg/kg IV is a common RSI choice; succinylcholine 1–2 mg/kg IV is an alternative when no contraindication exists. Start post-intubation analgesia/sedation immediately. Traumatic brain injury / raised ICP Primary goals are prevention of hypoxemia and hypotension, adequate analgesia, avoidance of agitation/coughing, normocapnia unless temporarily treating impending herniation, and preservation of the neurologic examination when feasible. Ketamine is not automatically contraindicated in acute brain injury and can be attractive when blood pressure is tenuous. Fentanyl provides analgesia; midazolam or short-acting sedatives may be added when needed. Propofol can reduce cerebral metabolic demand but hypotension is dangerous and prolonged/high-dose pediatric ICU infusion should be avoided. Neuromuscular blockade is reserved for a defined indication such as RSI, severe ventilator dyssynchrony or refractory ICP crises after adequate analgesia/sedation. It obscures the motor examination and seizure activity. Lines, chest tube and other painful bedside procedures Use local anesthetic whenever possible. For very painful procedures, ketamine is often a useful single-agent option; opioid plus sedative combinations can work but increase respiratory-depression risk. Chest-tube insertion generally requires strong analgesia plus sedation when time and physiology permit. For unstable children, titrate small doses and prioritize resuscitation. Imaging / non-painful immobility Use the least depth necessary. Dexmedetomidine or propofol may provide immobility depending on duration, airway risk and local credentialing; neither substitutes for analgesia when the procedure is painful. Reassess continuously because children can unintentionally progress to deeper sedation. Core monitoring Continuous pulse oximetry; frequent non-invasive blood pressure; ECG and capnography for IV moderate/deep sedation when available. Record drug, dose, route, time and response. Have age/size-appropriate airway equipment and reversal/rescue drugs immediately available. Sources Canadian Paediatric Society: Recommendations for procedural sedation in infants, children and adolescents. SCCM PANDEM pediatric pain, agitation and neuromuscular-blockade guideline; local PCCU/anesthesia formulary remains the dose authority. SEDATION BY PROCEDURE - Define procedure, pain, desired sedation depth and need for immobility. - Use local/regional analgesia whenever possible. - Choose one primary sedative strategy and titrate to effect. - Paralysis requires established analgesia + sedation and a defined indication. - Continuous monitoring and airway rescue capability are mandatory for deep sedation.

title: Intubation / RSI sedation
body: Intubation / RSI sedation Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Preparation Assign airway roles and plans A–D; optimize oxygenation, perfusion and glucose; prepare suction, BVM/PEEP, supraglottic rescue and waveform capnography. Anticipate peri-intubation hypotension. In shock, reduce sedative dose rather than giving a full healthy-child induction dose automatically. Analgesia / pretreatment Fentanyl 1–2 mcg/kg IV slow may be considered when analgesia or sympathetic blunting is desired and blood pressure allows. Rapid/high doses can cause apnea, hypotension and chest-wall rigidity. Routine lidocaine pretreatment to prevent ICP rise is not recommended; follow local neurocritical-care protocol for special circumstances. Induction options Ketamine 1–2 mg/kg IV. Often preferred for bronchospasm or relative hemodynamic instability; use a lower dose in catecholamine-depleted shock. Propofol 1–2 mg/kg IV in a hemodynamically stable child; consider substantially reduced dosing when preload/BP is marginal. Provides no analgesia. Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg IV is a rapid hemodynamically stable alternative; consider adrenal-suppression concerns, especially in septic shock. Paralysis Rocuronium 1–1.2 mg/kg IV for RSI. Longer duration than succinylcholine; ensure post-intubation sedation is ordered before paralysis wears off. Succinylcholine 1–2 mg/kg IV when appropriate. Avoid with known/suspected hyperkalemia-risk neuromuscular disease, major burns/crush after the risk window, malignant-hyperthermia susceptibility and other local contraindications. Immediately after tube placement Confirm sustained waveform ETCO2, then secure tube and reassess depth/position, oxygenation, ventilation and blood pressure. Begin analgesia and sedation immediately. Paralysis does not provide amnesia, anxiolysis or pain control. Sources PALS/local pediatric difficult-airway pathway; CPS procedural sedation principles; SCCM PANDEM principles for analgesia, sedation and NMBA use. PEDIATRIC RSI - Preoxygenate + optimize perfusion. - Induction: ketamine 1–2 mg/kg IV OR propofol 1–2 mg/kg IV if hemodynamically stable OR etomidate 0.3 mg/kg IV when appropriate. - Paralysis: rocuronium 1–1.2 mg/kg IV; succinylcholine 1–2 mg/kg IV when not contraindicated. - Confirm with waveform ETCO2. - Start post-intubation analgesia/sedation immediately.

title: TBI sedation & neuroprotection
body: TBI sedation & neuroprotection Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Neuroprotective priorities Avoid hypoxemia and hypotension; maintain age-appropriate cerebral perfusion, normothermia, normal glucose and ventilation targets. Elevate head midline when not contraindicated and treat seizures promptly. Sedation should prevent agitation, coughing and ventilator dyssynchrony without unnecessarily eliminating serial neurologic assessment. Analgesia Fentanyl 0.5–1 mcg/kg IV slow bolus is a common starting analgesic range; repeat/titrate carefully to physiology. Continuous infusion commonly begins around 0.5–1 mcg/kg/hr and is titrated per local PICU protocol. Avoid large rapid opioid boluses that cause hypotension or chest-wall rigidity. Sedation choices Ketamine: 1–2 mg/kg IV for induction; low-dose bolus/infusion can be used as an adjunct. Current practice no longer treats ketamine as universally contraindicated solely because of TBI; preserve blood pressure and use neurocritical-care guidance. Midazolam: 0.05–0.1 mg/kg IV titrated; useful for sedation/seizure control but can lower BP, accumulate and obscure the neurologic exam. Propofol: rapid onset/offset and decreases cerebral metabolic demand, but can cause significant hypotension. Avoid prolonged/high-dose continuous infusion for pediatric ICU sedation because of propofol infusion syndrome risk. Paralysis Use only for a defined indication such as RSI, refractory ICP crisis or severe ventilator dyssynchrony after adequate sedation/analgesia. Rocuronium is useful for RSI; cisatracurium may be useful for ongoing blockade when organ-independent elimination is desired. Use train-of-four plus clinical assessment and the lowest effective NMBA dose. Red flags New pupillary asymmetry, falling GCS, Cushing physiology, recurrent bradycardia/apnea, refractory hypoxemia/hypotension or seizures require immediate senior/neurosurgical/PCCU escalation. Sources CPS acute head trauma guidance; SCCM PANDEM; local pediatric neurocritical-care/TBI pathway. TBI SEDATION / NEUROPROTECTION - Prevent hypoxemia + hypotension. - Analgesia first; avoid agitation/coughing. - Ketamine is not automatically contraindicated in TBI; choose agent by physiology. - Avoid prolonged/high-dose propofol infusion in children. - NMBA only for a defined indication after deep analgesia/sedation; monitor blockade.

title: Lumbar puncture sedation
body: Lumbar puncture sedation Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Before sedation Confirm indication and contraindications, including concern for mass effect/herniation, clinically important coagulopathy, local infection and cardiorespiratory instability. Do not sedate an unstable child simply to complete the LP. Use topical anesthetic if time allows, local lidocaine, comfort positioning, distraction and caregiver/child-life support. Minimal / no sedation Older cooperative children may tolerate LP with excellent local anesthesia and coaching alone. Nitrous oxide or minimal anxiolysis may be an option where credentialing/equipment are available. Ketamine option Ketamine 1–1.5 mg/kg IV is a common initial dissociative sedation dose; additional 0.25–0.5 mg/kg IV doses may be titrated as needed under a procedural-sedation protocol. Provides analgesia plus dissociation. Watch for vomiting, hypersalivation, laryngospasm, apnea and recovery agitation; airway rescue equipment is mandatory. Propofol option Propofol 0.5–1 mg/kg IV titrated to effect can provide rapid deep sedation where appropriately credentialed. It has no analgesic effect, so maintain local anesthesia/analgesia. Important adverse effects are apnea/airway obstruction and hypotension; continuous capnography is strongly preferred for deep IV sedation. Opioid + benzodiazepine Fentanyl plus midazolam may provide analgesia/anxiolysis but has synergistic respiratory-depressant effects and often less reliable immobility than dissociative sedation. Titrate slowly with full monitoring. Paralysis Neuromuscular blockade is not indicated for routine lumbar puncture. If immobility cannot be safely achieved with sedation, stop and escalate to anesthesia/PCCU rather than paralyzing a spontaneously breathing child for an LP. Sources CPS procedural sedation statement; TREKK procedural sedation resources; local sedation credentialing and LP policy. LUMBAR PUNCTURE SEDATION - Local/topical anesthesia + comfort measures for every child when feasible. - Ketamine: 1–1.5 mg/kg IV initially, then 0.25–0.5 mg/kg IV titrated as needed under local protocol. - Propofol: 0.5–1 mg/kg IV titrated; provides sedation, not analgesia. - Avoid routine NMBA for LP. - Full deep-sedation monitoring and airway rescue capability.

title: Procedural sedation
body: Procedural sedation Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Safety framework Match drug choice to the procedure: painful versus non-painful, duration, need for immobility, airway risk, hemodynamics and practitioner familiarity. At least one clinician must be capable of advanced airway rescue; have suction, oxygen, BVM, airway adjuncts, emergency drugs and appropriate monitoring immediately available. Monitoring Continuous pulse oximetry and frequent non-invasive BP; ECG and end-tidal CO2 should be available for IV moderate/deep sedation. Record vitals, drug dose/time, depth and adverse events. Continue monitoring through recovery until the child has returned to baseline. Medication strategy Ketamine supplies both dissociation and analgesia. Propofol is a sedative-hypnotic without analgesia. Opioid + benzodiazepine combinations increase respiratory-depression risk. Avoid stacking repeated drugs without reassessing effect. Use one primary strategy and titrate deliberately. Escalation / anesthesia involvement Consider anesthesia for difficult airway, significant cardiorespiratory disease, severe OSA, very young/high-risk infants, ASA III or higher, active significant illness, increased ICP concern, or when local sedation criteria are not met. Sources Canadian Paediatric Society procedural sedation position statement; TREKK procedural sedation; local institutional sedation policy. PROCEDURAL SEDATION - Define procedure + target depth. - Confirm airway/resuscitation readiness and monitoring. - Choose one primary sedative strategy and titrate. - Treat pain separately when using a non-analgesic sedative. - Monitor through recovery to baseline.

title: Continuous analgesia
body: Continuous analgesia Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Clinical overview Continuous analgesia should use goal-directed, regularly reassessed sedation and analgesia rather than unstructured medication stacking. Initial stabilization Define pain/sedation target and reversible causes of distress. Use non-pharmacologic measures and family presence where appropriate. Disease-specific treatment / settings Prefer analgesia-first when pain is present; use validated scales and daily de-escalation. Neuromuscular blockade requires deep sedation, analgesia and eye/skin/pressure care. Monitoring Validated pain/sedation/delirium/withdrawal scores, respiratory status, BP and bowel/bladder function. Expected response Comfort and safety at target without excessive sedation. Failure criteria and escalation Escalating doses, delirium, withdrawal, hypotension or inability to awaken when expected. Complications / cautions Tolerance, withdrawal, delirium, immobility and prolonged ventilation. Sources and local verification SCCM PANDEM pediatric guidelines; local sedation protocol. title: Continuous sedation
body: Continuous sedation Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Clinical overview Set a patient-specific sedation target and prioritize analgesia-first, protocolized sedation with regular assessment. Medication doses / settings Common options include dexmedetomidine, midazolam, ketamine and opioid-based analgosedation; exact starting/titration doses require local PCCU/pharmacy protocol. Avoid prolonged propofol infusion in critically ill children because of propofol infusion syndrome risk. Minimize benzodiazepine exposure when feasible to reduce delirium risk. Monitoring intervals Use a validated sedation scale at regular intervals, pain scoring, delirium screening and daily review of ongoing need. Monitor hemodynamics, ventilation, drug accumulation, organ function and withdrawal risk. Failure criteria and escalation Agitation threatening devices despite addressing pain/delirium, oversedation, hypotension/bradycardia or escalating dose without effect. Sources and local verification SCCM PANDEM pediatric guidelines; local sedation and withdrawal protocols. title: Neuromuscular blockade
body: Neuromuscular blockade Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Clinical overview Use neuromuscular blockade only for a defined indication and shortest necessary duration. It does not provide analgesia, amnesia or sedation. Initial approach / settings Ensure adequate analgesia and sedation before and throughout paralysis; document indication and target depth. Use the lowest effective NMBA dose, daily reassessment and eye care. Monitoring intervals Clinical assessment plus train-of-four when appropriate; continuous ventilation and hemodynamic monitoring. Use EEG when seizure detection is required because clinical movement is suppressed. Failure criteria and escalation Unexpected movement, prolonged weakness, inability to monitor sedation, corneal injury or ventilator/physiologic deterioration. Complications / cautions Awareness, critical illness weakness, corneal injury, pressure injury and masked seizures. Sources and local verification SCCM PANDEM pediatric guidelines; local NMBA protocol. title: Fentanyl
body: Fentanyl Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Role Potent short-acting opioid for analgesia, procedural adjunct and ventilated-patient analgosedation. It does not provide reliable amnesia by itself. Typical pediatric IV reference doses Analgesic/procedural bolus: 0.5–1 mcg/kg IV slowly; selected intubation contexts may use 1–2 mcg/kg IV slowly. Continuous infusion: commonly 0.5–3 mcg/kg/hr, titrated to pain/sedation target and local protocol. Important adverse effects Respiratory depression/apnea, bradycardia, hypotension, ileus, urinary retention, nausea/pruritus, tolerance and withdrawal. Rapid or high-dose administration can cause chest-wall rigidity; give IV boluses slowly and be prepared to ventilate/paralyze if severe. Pearls Use lower/titrated dosing when combined with benzodiazepines, propofol or other sedatives. Renal dysfunction generally affects fentanyl less than morphine metabolites, but prolonged infusion can still accumulate. Sources SCCM PANDEM principles; local pediatric critical-care formulary/pharmacy. FENTANYL - Bolus 0.5–1 mcg/kg IV slow; selected RSI contexts 1–2 mcg/kg IV slow. - Infusion commonly 0.5–3 mcg/kg/hr. - Watch apnea, hypotension/bradycardia, ileus/urinary retention, tolerance/withdrawal and chest-wall rigidity. - Titrate to validated pain/sedation target.

title: Morphine
body: Morphine Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Clinical overview Morphine: opioid analgesic with histamine release and active metabolites; adjust in renal dysfunction. Always prescribe analgesia and sedation before or with paralysis. Initial stabilization Confirm indication, weight, airway plan, hemodynamics and concurrent sedatives. Use a validated sedation/pain target and the lowest effective dose. Disease-specific treatment / settings Use local formulary bolus/infusion doses and smart-pump concentrations. Daily reassessment and protocolized weaning reduce oversedation and withdrawal. Monitoring Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring; pain/sedation score, BP, ventilation, bowel/bladder function and drug-specific adverse effects. Expected response Comfort, synchrony and procedure tolerance at the predefined target. Failure criteria and escalation Inadequate comfort, hypotension, respiratory depression, delirium, prolonged paralysis or escalating requirements. Complications / cautions Tolerance, withdrawal, delirium, ileus, hypotension and prolonged ventilation. Sources and local verification SCCM PANDEM pediatric guidelines; local sedation formulary. title: Ketamine
body: Ketamine Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Role Dissociative anesthetic with analgesia, amnesia and bronchodilation; useful for painful procedures, RSI and as a PICU sedation adjunct. Airway reflexes are often preserved but not guaranteed; apnea, obstruction and laryngospasm can occur. Typical pediatric IV reference doses Procedural dissociation: 1–1.5 mg/kg IV initially; additional 0.25–0.5 mg/kg IV titrated as needed under a sedation protocol. RSI induction: 1–2 mg/kg IV; reduce in catecholamine-depleted shock. Analgesic/sub-dissociative bolus: 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV. PICU adjunct infusions vary widely; a common range is about 5–20 mcg/kg/min (0.3–1.2 mg/kg/hr), titrated per local protocol. Important adverse effects Hypersalivation, nausea/vomiting, recovery agitation/hallucinations, nystagmus, hypertension/tachycardia; uncommon laryngospasm or apnea. In profoundly catecholamine-depleted shock, direct myocardial depressant effects can become clinically important despite ketamine’s usual sympathomimetic profile. TBI / ICP pearl Ketamine is not considered universally contraindicated solely because of traumatic brain injury. In an unstable child, preservation of blood pressure may be advantageous; coordinate with neurocritical-care goals. Sources CPS procedural sedation principles; TREKK procedural sedation; SCCM PANDEM; local PCCU/anesthesia formulary. KETAMINE - Procedure: 1–1.5 mg/kg IV; top-ups 0.25–0.5 mg/kg IV. - RSI: 1–2 mg/kg IV; reduce in catecholamine-depleted shock. - Analgesic: 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV. - PICU adjunct infusion commonly ~5–20 mcg/kg/min per local protocol. - Watch secretions, vomiting, emergence reaction, laryngospasm/apnea and hemodynamic response.

title: Midazolam
body: Midazolam Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Role Benzodiazepine providing anxiolysis, amnesia, sedation and anticonvulsant effect. It does not provide analgesia. Typical pediatric IV reference doses Bolus: 0.05–0.1 mg/kg IV slowly, titrated to effect; use smaller doses when combined with opioids or in hemodynamic instability. Continuous infusion: commonly 0.05–0.2 mg/kg/hr in ventilated children, titrated to sedation target and local protocol. Important adverse effects Respiratory depression/apnea, hypotension, paradoxical agitation, delirium association, tolerance, accumulation with prolonged infusion and withdrawal. Pearls Respiratory depression is synergistic with opioids. Consider minimizing benzodiazepine exposure when alternatives meet the sedation goal. Sources SCCM PANDEM; local pediatric critical-care formulary/pharmacy. MIDAZOLAM - Bolus commonly 0.05–0.1 mg/kg IV slow. - Infusion commonly 0.05–0.2 mg/kg/hr. - No analgesia. - Watch apnea, hypotension, paradoxical agitation, delirium, accumulation and withdrawal.

title: Dexmedetomidine
body: Dexmedetomidine Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Role Alpha-2 agonist producing cooperative sedation and sympatholysis with relatively limited respiratory depression. Useful for ventilated patients and selected non-painful procedures. Typical pediatric infusion reference Continuous infusion is commonly 0.2–1.5 mcg/kg/hr. Many PICUs avoid a loading bolus because it can produce abrupt bradycardia/hypotension; follow local protocol. Important adverse effects Bradycardia, hypotension, transient hypertension with loading, reduced cardiac output in susceptible patients and withdrawal/rebound symptoms after prolonged use. Pearls Does not reliably provide adequate analgesia for painful procedures; pair with a pain strategy when pain is present. Sources SCCM PANDEM; local pediatric critical-care formulary/pharmacy. DEXMEDETOMIDINE - Infusion commonly 0.2–1.5 mcg/kg/hr. - Loading bolus often avoided in PICU. - Minimal respiratory depression compared with many sedatives but watch bradycardia/hypotension. - Add analgesia for painful procedures.

title: Propofol
body: Propofol Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Role Rapid sedative-hypnotic with fast onset/offset and antiemetic properties. It has no analgesic effect. Typical pediatric IV reference doses Procedural/deep sedation: 0.5–1 mg/kg IV titrated in small increments; some anesthesia inductions use 1–2 mg/kg IV depending on age and physiology. Reduce substantially in hypovolemia, shock or myocardial dysfunction. Continuous dosing should follow anesthesia/PICU protocol rather than a generic bedside range. Important adverse effects Apnea, airway obstruction, loss of protective reflexes, hypotension, bradycardia and pain on injection. Prolonged/high-dose pediatric ICU infusion is associated with propofol infusion syndrome; avoid using propofol as routine prolonged continuous PICU sedation. TBI pearl Can rapidly reduce cerebral metabolic demand but the benefit is lost if systemic hypotension compromises cerebral perfusion. Use only with close hemodynamic control. Sources CPS procedural sedation principles; pediatric anesthesia/PICU practice; local formulary. PROPOFOL - Procedural/deep sedation: commonly 0.5–1 mg/kg IV titrated. - Anesthesia induction often 1–2 mg/kg IV in stable physiology. - No analgesia. - Watch apnea/airway obstruction and hypotension. - Avoid routine prolonged/high-dose continuous PICU infusion in children because of PRIS risk.

title: Etomidate
body: Etomidate Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Role Ultra-short hypnotic used mainly for induction because it usually causes less cardiovascular depression than propofol. It has no analgesic effect. Typical pediatric IV reference dose Induction: 0.3 mg/kg IV is a commonly used reference dose; titrate/verify with local airway protocol. Important adverse effects Myoclonus, nausea/vomiting, pain on injection and transient adrenal suppression from 11β-hydroxylase inhibition. Because adrenal suppression may matter in septic shock, many pediatric critical-care teams prefer an alternative induction agent in sepsis; follow local practice. Sources Local pediatric RSI/anesthesia formulary; current pediatric critical-care practice. ETOMIDATE - Induction commonly 0.3 mg/kg IV. - Hemodynamically stable hypnotic; no analgesia. - Watch myoclonus and adrenal suppression; consider alternatives in septic shock per local protocol.

title: Rocuronium
body: Rocuronium Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Role Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Provides paralysis only—no analgesia, sedation or amnesia. Typical pediatric IV reference doses RSI: 1–1.2 mg/kg IV. Maintenance bolus: commonly 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV. Continuous infusion ranges vary by age and institution; titrate to clinical effect/train-of-four under a PICU protocol. Important adverse effects Prolonged weakness/paralysis, tachycardia in some patients, rare anaphylaxis and awareness if sedation is inadequate. Duration can be prolonged in organ dysfunction and after repeated dosing. Monitoring Confirm deep analgesia/sedation before and throughout paralysis. Use the lowest effective dose and train-of-four in conjunction with clinical assessment. Sources SCCM PANDEM; current local RSI/PICU formulary. ROCURONIUM - RSI: 1–1.2 mg/kg IV. - Maintenance bolus commonly 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV. - Paralysis only: establish analgesia + sedation first. - Use lowest effective dose; TOF + clinical assessment for ongoing blockade.

title: Succinylcholine
body: Succinylcholine Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Role Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker with very rapid onset and short duration. Provides paralysis only. Typical pediatric IV reference dose RSI/rescue airway: 1–2 mg/kg IV. IM dosing is institution-specific and should follow the emergency airway protocol. Major cautions Hyperkalemia and cardiac arrest risk in susceptible neuromuscular disease/denervation states and after major burns/crush injury; malignant-hyperthermia trigger; bradycardia is more common in children and with repeat dosing. Use only when contraindications have been considered and rescue capability is immediately available. Sources CPS procedural sedation rescue-medication table; local pediatric difficult-airway/RSI pathway. SUCCINYLCHOLINE - RSI/rescue airway: 1–2 mg/kg IV when appropriate. - Paralysis only—no sedation or analgesia. - Avoid/seek alternative in hyperkalemia-risk neuromuscular/denervation states, major burns/crush after risk develops, and malignant-hyperthermia susceptibility. - Watch bradycardia, especially repeat dosing.

title: Cisatracurium
body: Cisatracurium Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis Role Cisatracurium (Nimbex) is a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker with organ-independent Hofmann elimination, often useful when hepatic/renal dysfunction makes accumulation of other agents undesirable. It provides no analgesia, anxiolysis, sedation or amnesia. Typical pediatric IV reference doses Bolus: commonly 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV. Continuous infusion: commonly about 1–3 mcg/kg/min, titrated to the minimum blockade required and local PICU protocol. Important adverse effects Prolonged neuromuscular weakness, immobility complications, corneal injury/pressure injury risk and awareness if sedation is inadequate. Histamine-related hypotension/bronchospasm is less common than with atracurium but remains possible. Monitoring / care bundle Ensure continuous analgesia + sedation, eye lubrication/closure care, pressure-area care, DVT/mobility considerations as appropriate, and train-of-four plus clinical assessment. Sources SCCM PANDEM; local PICU/pharmacy neuromuscular-blockade protocol. CISATRACURIUM / NIMBEX - Bolus commonly 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV. - Infusion commonly ~1–3 mcg/kg/min. - Organ-independent Hofmann elimination. - Paralysis only: maintain deep analgesia + sedation. - TOF + clinical assessment; eye/skin/pressure care.

title: Hypernatremic dehydration
body: Hypernatremic dehydration Fluids & Electrolytes Clinical overview Hypernatremic dehydration requires confirmation of severity, chronicity, symptoms, renal function and ongoing losses before correction. Use trends and clinical context; avoid correcting a number in isolation. Initial stabilization Repeat/confirm critical results when safe, review ECG and medications, assess volume status and obtain strict intake/output. Call nephrology/PCCU early for severe symptoms, oliguria/anuria or rapidly changing values. Disease-specific treatment / settings Correct hypernatremic dehydration using the dedicated calculator or local replacement protocol when available. Account for enteral intake, carrier fluids, renal function and ongoing losses; use pharmacy-verified concentrations. Monitoring Serial electrolytes, renal function, ECG when relevant, urine output, fluid balance and neurologic status. Expected response Controlled correction with improving symptoms and no new electrolyte or volume complication. Failure criteria and escalation Neurologic symptoms, arrhythmia, worsening renal function, refractory abnormality or unsafe correction rate. Complications / cautions Overcorrection, arrhythmia, fluid overload, tissue injury from concentrated infusions and osmotic neurologic injury. Sources and local verification KDIGO pediatric principles; local electrolyte/renal protocol. title: DKA
body: DKA Endocrine & Metabolic Clinical overview Diagnose hyperglycemia with ketosis and metabolic acidosis; assess severity, dehydration, potassium and cerebral-injury risk. Initial stabilization Begin isotonic fluids, insulin infusion after initial fluid and potassium assessment, and frequent neurologic checks. Do not give insulin bolus. Disease-specific treatment / settings Add dextrose as glucose falls while continuing insulin to clear ketosis; replace potassium according to level, urine output and ECG. Monitoring Hourly glucose, frequent electrolytes/gas, corrected sodium trend, fluid balance, ECG when potassium abnormal and neurologic status. Expected response Closing anion gap/ketosis, improving acidosis and stable neurologic examination. Failure criteria and escalation Neurologic deterioration, shock, severe potassium abnormality, failure of acidosis to improve or hyperosmolar features. Complications / cautions Cerebral injury, hypokalemia, hypoglycemia, hyperchloremic acidosis and fluid overload. Sources and local verification ISPAD 2022/2024 DKA guidance; local pediatric DKA protocol. title: Cerebral edema in DKA
body: Cerebral edema in DKA Endocrine & Metabolic Clinical overview Treat suspected DKA-related cerebral injury immediately based on clinical findings; do not wait for imaging. Warning signs include headache, irritability, vomiting, slowing heart rate, rising BP, altered consciousness, cranial nerve abnormality or incontinence. Initial approach / settings Call PCCU, minimize stimulation, elevate head, ensure airway/oxygenation and reduce fluid rate if excessive while preserving perfusion. Continue insulin unless directed otherwise; avoid bicarbonate except specific resuscitation indications. Medication doses / settings Hypertonic saline 3% 5 mL/kg IV over 10–15 minutes (max per local protocol) OR mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg IV over 10–15 minutes. Repeat based on response and specialist direction. Monitoring intervals Neurologic observations at least hourly during DKA and more frequently when concerning; glucose hourly and electrolytes/gas every 2–4 hours per pathway. Failure criteria and escalation Progressive coma, abnormal pupils, seizures, respiratory failure or no response to initial osmotherapy. Prepare airway and neurocritical care transfer. Sources and local verification CPS/TREKK pediatric DKA guidance; ISPAD guidance; local endocrine/PCCU protocol. title: Septic shock
body: Septic shock Sepsis & Infection Clinical overview Suspect shock when infection is accompanied by abnormal perfusion, altered mental status, oliguria, hypotension or lactate elevation. Hypotension is late in children. Initial stabilization Obtain cultures without delaying antibiotics, give broad-spectrum antimicrobials promptly, establish IV/IO access and reassess perfusion repeatedly. Use cautious aliquots of isotonic crystalloid with reassessment, especially where myocardial dysfunction or resource limitations exist. Disease-specific treatment / settings Start epinephrine or norepinephrine early when shock persists despite initial fluid or when fluid overload risk is high; peripheral initiation is acceptable with vigilant site monitoring under protocol. Monitoring HR, BP, capillary refill, pulses, temperature gradient, mental status, urine output, lactate trend and bedside cardiac function. Expected response Improved perfusion, mental status, urine output and falling lactate/vasoactive requirement. Failure criteria and escalation Persistent shock, rising lactate, myocardial dysfunction, escalating vasoactives or organ failure. Complications / cautions Fluid overload, arrhythmia, limb ischemia, ARDS and multiorgan dysfunction. Sources and local verification Surviving Sepsis Campaign pediatric guidelines; local sepsis pathway. title: Acetaminophen
body: Acetaminophen Toxicology Clinical overview Acetaminophen toxicity requires stabilization, toxidrome recognition and early poison-centre consultation. Dose, timing, formulation, co-ingestants and intent materially change management. Initial stabilization ABCDE, bedside glucose, ECG, temperature and targeted laboratory testing. title: Lumbar puncture
body: Lumbar puncture Procedures Clinical checklist Confirm indication, consent/emergency authority, patient identity, weight, allergies and contraindications. Assess for signs suggesting raised ICP/mass lesion, cardiorespiratory instability, local infection and clinically important coagulopathy. Use sterile technique, appropriate needle length, positioning and an assistant. Consider ultrasound to identify landmarks when expertise is available. Analgesia and sedation Use topical/local anesthesia plus comfort measures whenever feasible. For a detailed medication strategy open “Lumbar puncture sedation” under Sedation, Analgesia & Paralysis. Ketamine is often suitable when deep sedation plus analgesia is required; propofol requires a separate analgesia/local-anesthetic plan. Routine neuromuscular blockade is not appropriate for LP. Monitoring If sedated: use the institutional procedural-sedation monitoring standard, including continuous oxygenation and ventilation assessment. Document attempts, specimen appearance and complications. Failure / escalation Stop and reassess for cardiorespiratory deterioration, new neurologic concern, repeated failed attempts, significant bleeding or inability to provide safe sedation. Escalate to anesthesia/PCCU/experienced proceduralist as appropriate. Sources CPS procedural sedation guidance; local lumbar-puncture and sedation policies. title: Mild pain
body: Mild pain Assessment Use self-report whenever developmentally possible (numeric rating, Faces scale); use FLACC or another validated behavioural tool when self-report is not reliable. Identify pain mechanism, severity, functional impact, prior analgesia, allergies, hepatic/renal disease and bleeding risk. Initial treatment Comfort positioning, explanation, distraction, heat/ice when appropriate and caregiver involvement. Acetaminophen 10–15 mg/kg PO every 4–6 hours as needed; do not exceed the lower of 75 mg/kg/day or the institutional maximum. Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg PO every 6–8 hours as needed (usual maximum 400 mg/dose); avoid with significant dehydration, renal impairment, GI bleeding or NSAID contraindication. Reassessment Reassess pain and function within 30–60 minutes after oral medication and after any clinical change. Escalate if pain remains moderate/severe, diagnosis is uncertain, or red flags are present.

title: Moderate pain
body: Moderate pain Approach Continue non-pharmacologic measures and schedule acetaminophen/NSAID when safe. For acute moderate pain, intranasal fentanyl can provide rapid analgesia while IV access is being established. Medication options Fentanyl intranasal 1–2 micrograms/kg (usual maximum 100 micrograms total), divided between nostrils; monitor sedation and respiration. Morphine PO 0.2–0.5 mg/kg every 4–6 hours (usual maximum 15 mg/dose), starting at the lower end in opioid-naive patients. Ketorolac 0.5 mg/kg IV every 6–8 hours may be used when appropriate; use local age/dose maximums and avoid renal/GI bleeding risk. Monitoring Document pain score, sedation score, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and response. Avoid codeine in children and adolescents.

title: Severe pain
body: Severe pain Immediate priorities Treat severe pain promptly while identifying time-critical causes such as compartment syndrome, ischemia, torsion, intracranial pathology, perforation or sepsis. Use continuous pulse oximetry and frequent sedation/respiratory assessment when parenteral opioids are used. Parenteral options Morphine IV 0.05–0.1 mg/kg slowly; reassess and titrate using local maximums and opioid-naive precautions. Fentanyl IV 0.5–1 microgram/kg slowly may be preferred when rapid titration or less histamine release is desired. Consider PCA or nurse-controlled analgesia with a standardized institutional protocol for ongoing severe pain. Escalation Escalate to senior/PCCU/anesthesia or acute pain service for uncontrolled pain, increasing opioid requirement, respiratory depression, hemodynamic instability or diagnostic uncertainty.

title: Oral versus IV options
body: Oral versus IV options Choose the route Prefer oral therapy when the child can absorb and tolerate it and rapid titration is not required. Use intranasal analgesia when fast, needle-free treatment is needed. Use IV therapy for severe pain, shock, persistent vomiting, impaired absorption or when rapid titration is required. Principles Do not delay analgesia solely while waiting for IV access. Use multimodal analgesia to reduce opioid exposure. Convert to oral therapy as soon as pain and physiology permit.

title: Sickle-cell vaso-occlusive pain
body: Sickle-cell vaso-occlusive pain First hour Assess promptly and initiate analgesia within 30–60 minutes. Exclude acute chest syndrome, infection, sequestration, osteomyelitis, avascular necrosis and other causes. Give intranasal fentanyl 1–2 micrograms/kg (maximum 100 micrograms) when appropriate, followed by oral or IV opioid according to response. Ongoing treatment Schedule acetaminophen and one NSAID when not contraindicated; do not combine oral and IV NSAIDs. Morphine PO 0.2–0.5 mg/kg every 4–6 hours or IV 0.1 mg/kg slowly with reassessment; use patient-specific plans and local maxima. Use maintenance—not hyperhydration—when IV fluids are needed; encourage oral intake, mobility, heat, incentive spirometry and bowel prophylaxis. Monitoring and escalation Monitor SpO2, respiratory symptoms, fever and sedation. Chest, back or abdominal pain requires vigilance for acute chest syndrome. Consult hematology for refractory pain, PCA/infusion, transfusion questions or complications.

title: SJS/TEN pain
body: SJS/TEN pain Priorities Treat as a dermatologic critical illness: stop suspected culprit drugs, involve dermatology/burn/PCCU early, protect skin and mucosa and minimize shear. Pain may be severe and include cutaneous, ocular, oral and genitourinary components. Analgesia Use scheduled acetaminophen when safe plus titrated IV opioid for severe pain. Procedural pain (dressings, line care, examination) often requires anticipatory analgesia and sometimes procedural sedation. Avoid NSAIDs when renal injury, bleeding or the suspected culprit medication makes them unsafe. Monitoring Continuous respiratory monitoring with escalating opioids; assess hydration, temperature, infection, ocular pain and urinary retention. Early ophthalmology and site-specific mucosal care are essential.

title: Neuropathic pain
body: Neuropathic pain Recognition Burning, shooting, electric pain, allodynia or hyperalgesia suggests a neuropathic component. Assess for nerve injury, infection, chemotherapy toxicity, spinal pathology and complex regional pain. Management Use rehabilitation, sleep support and psychological strategies alongside medication. Gabapentin or pregabalin may be considered with pain/neurology/pharmacy input; start low, titrate slowly and adjust for renal function. Avoid abrupt discontinuation after sustained therapy. Escalation Refer persistent or function-limiting pain to a pediatric chronic pain service.

title: Post-operative pain
body: Post-operative pain Multimodal plan Use scheduled acetaminophen and NSAID when permitted by the procedure and patient factors. Use regional/local anesthetic techniques and non-pharmacologic measures when available. Reserve opioids for breakthrough moderate–severe pain and use the lowest effective dose. Reassessment Assess pain at rest and with movement, sedation, nausea, pruritus, urinary retention, bowel function and respiratory status. Escalate unexpectedly severe or increasing pain because it may indicate a surgical complication.

title: Opioid monitoring
body: Opioid monitoring Before dosing Confirm weight, opioid exposure, sleep-disordered breathing, neuromuscular disease, renal/hepatic function and concurrent sedatives. Record baseline pain, sedation score, respiratory rate, SpO2 and blood pressure. After dosing Reassess after IV dosing within minutes and after oral dosing within the expected onset window. Use continuous pulse oximetry for high-risk children or repeated/parenteral dosing; capnography may be useful when deeply sedated or receiving PCA. Sedation usually precedes respiratory arrest—hold opioid and escalate for increasing somnolence, snoring/obstruction, bradypnea or desaturation.

title: Naloxone rescue
body: Naloxone rescue Immediate response Call for help, open and support the airway, provide oxygen/ventilation and stop opioid administration. For clinically significant opioid-induced respiratory depression, use naloxone according to the local resuscitation/formulary protocol. Dose concepts A common emergency dose is 0.1 mg/kg IV/IM/IN in younger children or when complete reversal is required, subject to institutional maximums. For iatrogenic oversedation where analgesia should be preserved, smaller titrated IV doses may be used under senior supervision. After reversal Observe for recurrent toxicity because naloxone may wear off before the opioid. Repeat dosing or infusion may be required. Expect acute pain, vomiting, agitation or withdrawal in opioid-tolerant patients.

title: Opioid conversion
body: Opioid conversion Safety principles Equianalgesic tables are estimates and vary by age, route, opioid exposure and clinical state. Calculate the total opioid dose over the previous 24 hours, convert using an institutional pediatric table, then reduce the calculated new opioid dose for incomplete cross-tolerance—often by 25–50%—unless pain severity requires specialist adjustment. Do not automate Avoid direct conversion of methadone, transdermal fentanyl or high-dose/chronic regimens without pain/palliative care/pharmacy expertise. Reassess frequently after any conversion and provide a rescue-dose plan.

title: Sedation and respiratory-risk check
body: Sedation and respiratory-risk check High-risk features Age under 6 months, obstructive sleep apnea, obesity, craniofacial anomaly, neuromuscular weakness, lung disease, renal/hepatic dysfunction, opioid naivety, concurrent benzodiazepine/antihistamine/gabapentinoid or escalating opioid dose. Actions Use the lowest effective dose, avoid stacking sedatives, choose enhanced monitoring and ensure naloxone/airway equipment are available. Obtain senior/PCCU/anesthesia review when risk is high or sedation is increasing.

title: Escalation guide
body: Airway Stridor with fatigue, drooling/tripod posture, rapidly progressive swelling, recurrent apnea, inability to protect the airway, tracheostomy obstruction/dislodgement, or anticipated difficult airway. Breathing Severe work of breathing, silent/poor air entry, persistent hypoxemia, rapidly rising oxygen/HFNC/NIV, hypercapnia, recurrent apnea, or exhaustion. Circulation Shock, hypotension, weak pulses, abnormal perfusion, arrhythmia with poor perfusion, hypertensive emergency, major hemorrhage, or rapidly accumulating fluid overload. Neurologic Declining GCS, unequal pupils, focal deficit, status epilepticus, suspected cerebral injury/raised ICP, or acute bilirubin encephalopathy. Metabolic / renal Recurrent hypoglycemia, dangerous sodium/potassium/calcium, severe acidosis, anuria, pulmonary edema, or likely dialysis indication. Hematology / oncology Hyperleukocytosis symptoms, tumor lysis, DIC, acute chest syndrome deterioration, splenic sequestration, or severe transfusion reaction. Surgery / trauma Peritonitis, bilious vomiting with deterioration, ischemic limb/compartment signs, significant head/abdominal injury, or immediate safeguarding risk. Unit capability The child needs monitoring, oxygen, ventilation, vasoactive support, staffing, procedures, or reassessment frequency beyond the receiving unit. Escalate immediately Call the senior/staff and required bedside team at the same time when delay could harm the child.
